terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation (-iō): with the accusative, often with an ablative of the state produced
evidence: Cic. Fam. 16.4.1: variē sum adfectus tuīs litterīs
Liv. 28.15: famēs sitisque corpora adficerent (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to do something to one, i.e. to exert an influence on body or mind, so that it is brought into such or such a state”. Passive: be affected, often with an ablative: dolōre afficī, to feel pain (Traupman 105, 152); morbō affectus, ill. Where “affect” means “concern, apply to”, see concern (be about, matter to): attinet, pertinet ad.

evidence: Cic. Fam. 3.10.1: graviter prīmō nūntiō commōtus sum
terms.comment: Of news and events that disturb the mind; Augustine uses it of being moved to tears.

phrases.latin: Variē sum adfectus tuīs litterīs, valdē priōre pāginā perturbātus, paulum alterā recreātus.
phrases.english: Your letter affected me in two ways: the first page upset me badly, the second cheered me up a little.

phrases.latin: etsī graviter prīmō nūntiō commōtus sum
phrases.english: although I was badly shaken by the first news

phrases.latin: quantum flēvī in hymnīs et canticīs tuīs, suāve sonantis ecclēsiae tuae vōcibus commōtus ācriter!
phrases.english: how I wept at your hymns and songs, deeply moved by the voices of your sweetly singing church!

sources: Lewis & Short: afficio · Lewis & Short: commoveo · Lewis & Short: moveo
